title: Berkshire 1991 letter: franchises vs businesses, See's lessons, and why Buffett concentrates in great companies
summary: Buffett explains how look-through earnings, franchise economics (See's, media), owner-style manager compensation and cheap float drive Berkshire's value. He also sets his acquisition criteria, defends a concentrated hold-forever portfolio, and confesses the $1.4B Fannie Mae omission error.

principles.text: Judge your portfolio by look-through earnings a decade out; think about businesses, not stock prices.
principles.quote: The goal of each investor should be to create a portfolio (in effect, a "company") that will deliver him or her the highest possible look-through earnings a decade or so from now.

principles.text: A true franchise has needed product, no close substitute and no price regulation, so it can price aggressively and tolerate poor management.
principles.quote: An economic franchise arises from a product or service that: (1) is needed or desired; (2) is thought by its customers to have no close substitute and; (3) is not subject to price regulation.

principles.text: A mere business earns exceptional profits only as low-cost operator or under tight supply, and can be killed by bad management.
principles.quote: In contrast, "a business" earns exceptional profits only if it is the low-cost operator or if supply of its product or service is tight.

principles.text: Small changes in growth assumptions can cut a valuation by more than half, so expectations matter enormously.
principles.quote: Thus a seemingly modest shift in assumptions reduces the property's valuation to 10 times after-tax earnings (or about 6 1/2 times pre-tax earnings).

principles.text: Profit growth must be judged against the incremental capital needed to produce it; See's grew hugely on tiny reinvestment.
principles.quote: For an increase in profits to be evaluated properly, it must be compared with the incremental capital investment required to produce it.

principles.text: Seek great, understandable businesses with able managers; avoid trading portions of far-from-great businesses.
principles.quote: Charlie and I are simply not smart enough, considering the large sums we work with, to get great results by adroitly buying and selling portions of far-from-great businesses.
